title: Change these iOS privacy settings to lock your iPhone from prying eyes
content:
Macworld

iPhones are equipped with some of the best privacy protections in the industry, and unlike many rivals, Apple doesn’t make its money from selling your personal data. When you buy an iPhone or a Mac, you know your most sensitive data is safely locked away from prying eyes, even Apple’s.

But despite that, there are ways you can enhance your privacy even further by tweaking a few settings and features. Here, we’ll look at the things you can do to bolster your privacy and security on iOS, but many of these same principles apply to Apple’s other platforms. Make these changes and enable these features, and you’ll be taking some serious steps towards keeping your private info safe and secure.

Stop apps in their tracks

Foundry

Great privacy starts with ensuring the apps you use on your iPhone are behaving themselves. Before you download an app, you can check the App Store’s “nutrition labels” to learn what private information each app collects about you. Just go to the App Store page for the app in question and scroll down to the App Privacy section.

Another way you can keep apps in line is by using App Tracking Transparency. When you first open a freshly downloaded app, you’ll often be greeted with a pop-up window explaining that the app wants to “track your activity across other companies’ apps and websites.” Select the Ask App Not to Track option, and you’ll ensure it can’t follow you once you leave the app.

Finally, you can catch up on all the ways your data has been shared with apps on your iPhone by opening the Settings app and heading to Privacy & Security > App Privacy Report. This breaks down the requests made for your info–data and sensor access, network activity, and more–by various apps. You can disable or re-enable this report at the bottom of the page.

Close the windows into email and the web

Two activities tend to occupy most of the time spent on our iPhones: the web and email. They’re also two ways we can have our privacy violated. Thankfully, Apple has put measures in place to help combat that.

We’ll start with web browsing. If you use Safari, it comes with a feature called Intelligent Tracking Prevention. This blocks cross-site tracking, which is a technique used by websites and data brokers to follow you around the web in order to learn as much about you as possible. The end goal is to sell you products and personalized advertising.

Intelligent Tracking Prevention puts a stop to this by hiding your IP address, preventing these sites from building a profile of you. It’s on by default, but if you want to check, go to Settings > Apps > Safari and enable the toggle next to Prevent Cross-Site Tracking. Underneath this toggle is Hide IP Address; tap this and ensure the setting reads Trackers and Websites.

Foundry

Apple has a few other ways to protect yourself online. When you need to create an online account, you can use the Sign in with Apple option whenever it’s available. This gives you a random email address and redirects messages to your inbox, preventing your actual email address from being signed up to newsletters and spam mail without your permission. You can see which sites and apps you’ve used Sign in with Apple on by going to Settings > [Your Name] > Sign in with Apple.

If you pay for an iCloud+ subscription, you get access to a few other privacy-protecting features. That includes iCloud Private Relay, which ensures that no one (not even Apple) can see both your IP address and the sites you’re visiting at the same time. To enable it, go to Settings > [Your Name] > iCloud > Private Relay, then flip the Private Relay toggle on.

Another iCloud+ feature is Hide My Email. Like Sign in with Apple, this generates a random email address to use when signing up for a website account. The difference is that Hide My Email is offered even if a website doesn’t use Sign in with Apple, ensuring you’re never left without protection. To use it, select the Hide My Email option whenever you type in an email field. You can also use it in the Mail app by tapping the From field. To see where you’ve used it or to create a new email address, open the Settings app and head to [Your Name] > iCloud > Hide My Email.

You can keep your data under lock and key in the Mail app by using Mail Privacy Protection. According to Apple, this “Hides your IP address so senders can’t link it to your other online activity or determine your exact location. It also prevents senders from seeing if you’ve opened the email message they sent you.” You can enable it in Settings > Apps > Mail > Privacy Protection > Protect Mail Activity.

Lock it all down

What about the possibility of someone stealing your phone or one of your login credentials? For that, you need to make sure your phone and accounts are fully locked down. One of the most straightforward options is to enable Face ID, which can be done in Settings > Face ID & Passcode. This is one of the most secure ways to keep your private docs safely protected behind biometric verification.

Also, you can require two-factor authentication for your Apple Account in Settings > [Your Name] > Sign-In & Security > Two-Factor Authentication. Modern iPhones require a six-digit passcode, but you can increase this and optionally mix in alphanumeric characters in Face ID & Passcode settings by selecting “Change Passcode,” entering your PIN, then choosing Passcode Options.

Foundry

Despite requiring a passcode, your Lock Screen can still give would-be thieves and malcontents a lot of information. For example, the Control Center is accessible without entering a passcode, so someone could disable Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and cellular data, which in turn would prevent Find My from working, effectively disabling your device tracking. To prevent that, go to Settings > Face ID & Passcode, then scroll down to the Allow Access When Locked section and disable the toggle next to Control Center. While there, you might want to also disable access to Workout Health Data to keep this section of your personal info under wraps.

Speaking of thieves, new iPhones come with Stolen Device Protection by default, which requires a user to pass a biometric test (such as Face ID or Touch ID authentication) to perform certain tasks when your iPhone is in an unfamiliar location. To ensure it’s enabled, go to Settings > Face ID & Passcode > Stolen Device Protection, then make sure the toggle is on next to Stolen Device Protection.

Apple added a Lockdown Mode to iOS recently. This is for the most serious cases of compromised data, where a user suspects they are being targeted by a nation-state or other powerful actor. Hopefully you won’t need it, but if you do, you can enable it in Settings > Privacy & Security > Lockdown Mode. Note that this limits functionality for some apps and features.

Hide your location

Foundry

Your location can give away an awful lot about you, and that can often be used for nefarious purposes. That’s why you shouldn’t just hand out a blanket pass to any apps that demand to know your precise location. When an app asks for this data, think about whether it actually needs it, and only permit it if you feel it’s necessary for the app’s operation.

To see which apps have access to your location, open the Settings app and navigate to Privacy & Security > Location Services. Tap an app to see what permissions it has; you can choose between Never; Ask Next Time or When I Share; While Using the App; and Always (not every app has all of these options, but you’ll see at least a couple). You can also choose to share your precise whereabouts, or a more privacy-friendly vague location instead.

Similarly, you can see which apps have requested access to your iPhone’s camera and microphones by going to Settings > Privacy & Security, then choosing either Camera or Microphone. As with your location data, access to these sensors should be granted judiciously and only when necessary. Disable it for any apps that you don’t feel comfortable giving access to.

Stop unwanted trackers

Apple

This section is not related to you giving permission to something. Quite the opposite, in fact. We’ve seen in the press numerous instances of people using an AirTag to track (and stalk) an unwitting victim, which has obvious risks to privacy and safety. Thankfully, Apple has implemented a system that can alert you to an AirTag or other tracker that is logging your location when it shouldn’t be.

Note that this works with any AirTag, set of AirPods, Find My network accessory, or compatible Bluetooth tracker, so you should be alerted no matter what’s being used, as long as it can be used with an iPhone.

First, you need to have location services turned on in Settings > Privacy & Security > Location Services. From here, tap System Services and enable both Find My iPhone and Significant Locations & Routes. Apple also says that both Bluetooth and notifications need to be switched on, and you can’t be using airplane mode. If all that’s in place, you’ll get a notification whenever your iPhone notices that an unknown AirTag or other tracker is traveling with you.

If that happens, the Find My app will show you where the tracker has been detected and the route it has taken with you. To find it, tap the alert, then select Continue > Play Sound to have the tracker buzz, if possible–follow the sound to find it. You might also see a Find Nearby option, which can also guide you to the tracker.

If the tracker you discover turns out to be an AirTag, you can hold your iPhone to the AirTag’s white side until a notification appears. Tap it to see info on the AirTag’s owner, including the last four digits of their phone number. To disable the tracker (regardless of its type) and prevent it from trailing you any further, open the Find My app and go to Items > Items Detected With You. Tap the unknown tracker, pick Instructions to Disable, then follow the on-screen instructions.

Make your iPhone a one-way street

Many apps (and Apple) collect analytics data to help improve their products. Sometimes, though, this information is also used to build a profile of you and serve you personalized ads. Whatever the case, you might want to disable that data collection to keep your privacy protected.

Foundry

To do so, go to Settings > Privacy & Security > Analytics & Improvements, then disable the toggles for any information you don’t feel comfortable sharing. Next, go back to Privacy & Security, then choose Apple Advertising and disable the toggle next to Personalized Ads. While this won’t cut down the number of ads you’ll see, it should stop Apple from gathering info on you and using it to build a profile.
